video_title: So, how about those midterm elections?
gist: Volts host David Roberts and Climate Cabinet's Caroline Spears dissect the 2026 Democratic 'blue nami' (House, ~55-56 Senate seats, up to 22 state trifectas, Texas statewide sweep) through a climate/energy lens: new trifectas and utility commissions, a bipartisan data center backlash, utility ballot measures, and the challenge of delivering lower energy costs before 2028.

insights.claim: Democrats won the US House by a 30+ seat margin (about 25 Republican-to-Democrat flips, the biggest House gain since 1990) and hold 54 certain Senate seats with Alaska and Mississippi outstanding, putting 55-56 seats in play.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: A near filibuster-proof Senate plus House control reopens federal energy, tariff and permitting legislation that markets had priced as gridlocked.

insights.claim: Democrats are on track for about 30 governorships including every swing state, covering more than 75% of the US population, and state trifectas rose from 16 to as many as 22.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: State-level policy (utility regulation, clean energy procurement, data center rules) now tilts toward Democratic priorities across most of the US population.
insights.quote: the biggest and most dramatic political reversal of my lifetime

insights.claim: 54% of Americans now live in a state with a Democratic trifecta, an outcome Roberts says no one predicted weeks before the election.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Majority of US load and population now sits under governments able to pass clean energy and utility reform without divided-government friction.
insights.quote: 54% of Americans now live in a state with a democratic trifecta

insights.claim: Every statewide office up in Texas went Democratic, the first Democratic statewide wins since 1994, including Gina Hinojosa as governor and the Texas House flipping, while the Texas Senate stayed Republican.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: ERCOT-state energy policy and the culture-war pushback against renewables in Texas could ease; watch Texas legislation in 2027.

insights.claim: Climate Cabinet backed 120+ state and local races in 10+ states, won over 100, lost 10, with 10 too close to call, and saw candidates win even in R+16 to R+18 districts it had targeted as long shots.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Shows the depth of the swing reached deep-red districts, implying many inexperienced new legislators who are open to lobbying and policy education before January.
insights.quote: we were involved in over 120 races across more than 10 states on Tuesday. We won over 100 of them.

insights.claim: Roberts frames the election as a cost-of-living backlash driven most visibly by a war with Iran that pushed up gasoline and diesel prices, with electricity bills a secondary driver.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Political risk now attaches to energy price levels; incumbents of either party face punishment for rising pump and power prices.

insights.claim: Gerrymandering-driven mid-decade redistricting (e.g., Texas redrawing for Trump) backfired, and Roberts sees a federal anti-gerrymandering bill as now a real possibility.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Structural electoral reform could make Democratic gains stickier, affecting long-run policy durability assumptions.

themes.theme: New trifectas and state clean energy agendas

insights.claim: Climate Cabinet targeted five trifecta opportunities (Minnesota, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Arizona) and all flipped, plus Nevada; Arizona has its first Democratic trifecta since 1966.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Expect a burst of clean energy, transportation electrification and utility bills in these states in 2027 sessions.
insights.quote: First dem trifecta in Arizona since 1966.

insights.claim: Spears sees Arizona as the biggest upside opportunity because the sunniest state has badly underbuilt solar and batteries relative to potential; at her prior solar company more projects were built in Massachusetts than in Arizona.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Arizona solar and storage developers and suppliers could see a policy-driven acceleration in deployment.

insights.claim: Pennsylvania gets only about 3% of its electricity from renewables, is a bottom-five state, and its Senate has blocked clean energy bills for decades, so a Democratic trifecta there represents large untapped battery and renewable potential.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: PJM-region renewable and storage developers may gain a newly permissive Pennsylvania market.
insights.quote: because the state Senate has been where clean energy bills go to die for 40 years

insights.claim: Governor Shapiro has already said funding for Pennsylvania's zero-carbon transit and transportation system is a top priority to pass in the next couple of months, with housing also on his first list.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Near-term Pennsylvania transit funding legislation is a concrete catalyst to track.

insights.claim: Minnesota's earlier cautious trifecta passed little and lost reelection, while its 2022 trifecta went big; both speakers argue new trifectas should be ambitious because voters demanded big change on costs.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Expect aggressive, fast legislative agendas in new trifecta states rather than incrementalism.

insights.claim: In Michigan, the state House member who authored the bill to repeal Michigan's clean energy law lost his seat, after two years of rollback attempts against Michigan's 100% clean standard.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Reduces repeal risk for Michigan's clean electricity standard, supporting long-dated renewable procurement there.

insights.claim: The North Carolina House flipped for the first time since 2010 and the state Senate hinges on about 300 provisional votes; the legislature controls redistricting in a heavily gerrymandered state.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: A possible seventh new trifecta would add a Duke Energy-territory state to the reform column.

insights.claim: Democratic governors in every swing state create a firewall against attempts to manipulate the 2028 election.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Lowers tail risk of contested-election chaos in 2028.

insights.claim: Democrats won a 3-2 majority on the Georgia Public Service Commission, with Peter Hubbard part of the new majority alongside a Democratic governor.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Georgia utility rate cases, gas plant buildout and cost recovery decisions could turn against the incumbent utility; a regulatory risk to watch.

insights.claim: Spears targets construction-work-in-progress financing, which lets utilities charge customers while building plants (as Georgia did with Vogtle) and is sometimes available only for gas plants, not solar or batteries.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: New regulators hostile to CWIP threaten a favorable cost-recovery mechanism for utility gas plant capex.
insights.quote: they can charge you while they are building the gas plant

insights.claim: Democrats flipped two seats on the Arizona Corporation Commission (from 5-0 to 3-2 Republican), putting a Democratic majority one seat away in 2028; Turning Point USA lost here after also losing at Salt River Project.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Arizona utility regulation could flip in 2028, a medium-term risk/opportunity for Arizona utilities and solar.

insights.claim: Louisiana's Public Service Commission moved further Republican, from 3-2 to 4-1, despite voter anger over data centers and power bills.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Louisiana remains a friendlier regulatory venue for data center buildout than newly blue states.

insights.claim: A Democrat, mechanical engineer John Rosenthal, won a Texas Railroad Commission seat (now 2-1 Republican), the first Democratic seat on the oil and gas regulator since 1994, after Bo French ran a campaign about stopping Sharia law.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Adds an expert minority voice on Texas oil and gas regulation; mostly symbolic near term.

insights.claim: Down-ballot utility commission races still show significant undervoting, where voters skip PSC/PUC contests, which Spears flags as a key risk to future consumer-focused wins.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Regulator outcomes may revert in less wave-like years; do not assume the new PSC majorities are durable.

insights.claim: Spears argues utility ownership structure (municipal, co-op, investor-owned) matters less than transparency and government capacity, citing TVA's high rates driven by keeping coal online and 100+ public power agencies locked into Illinois' Prairie State coal plant via undisclosed contracts.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Municipalization is not automatically a clean or low-cost path; judge utilities on oversight and accountability.
insights.quote: it all matters on government capacity

insights.claim: Roughly 40 local ballot measures to ban, pause or restrict data centers nearly all passed, with about 80% votes in places like Joliet, Illinois, and the issue is strongly bipartisan.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Siting risk for hyperscale data centers has become a ballot-box issue; expect slower, costlier site approvals.

insights.claim: 20 of 36 gubernatorial candidates promised some kind of data center moratorium, and nearly all 120+ Climate Cabinet candidates named data centers when asked how climate policy can lower costs.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: State-level moratoria and cost-allocation rules are a material headwind for AI infrastructure capex plans.
insights.quote: It was the most unanimous response I've ever seen from doing this work over five years.

insights.claim: Elon Musk spent about half a billion dollars backing pro-AI and pro-data-center candidates and did poorly on election night.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Money from the AI industry is not buying political protection; political risk for AI buildout is rising.
insights.quote: Elon Musk spent about half a billion dollars backing pro AI and pro data center candidates and did not have a good night.

insights.claim: Data centers poll roughly 75/25 unfavorable, worse than typical NIMBY opposition to clean energy, because they are a physical manifestation of AI-driven economic anxiety and job-loss fears.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Opposition is structural, not a PR problem, so community-benefit and cost-coverage concessions will be needed to site projects.
insights.quote: Data centers are a physical manifestation of economic anxiety that people have around AI.

insights.claim: Battery storage projects are already drawing opposition because they resemble data centers, creating risk that clean energy and transmission get lumped in with data center backlash.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Storage developers face spillover siting risk from anti-data-center sentiment.

insights.claim: Ohio governor-elect Amy Acton wants a data center moratorium unless facilities cover 100% of their utility costs, and Roberts urges states to make cash-rich data centers fund grid upgrades before an AI bubble pops.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Large-load tariffs shifting grid costs to data centers raise hyperscaler power costs while benefiting grid buildout.
insights.quote: let's get useful policies passed and useful steel in the ground with their money before the bubble pops cuz that stuff will last

insights.claim: Having local officials sign NDAs with data center developers is seen as a major driver of community anger, and Spears calls for a complete rethink of community engagement.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Developers offering transparency and community benefits may win sites competitors lose.

insights.claim: Michigan Proposal 2, which bans utilities from spending money in politics, passed with about 84% of the vote and is already facing a legal challenge.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Curbs utility political influence; similar bills may spread to other legislatures.
insights.quote: bans Michigan utilities from putting money in politics

insights.claim: A gas-industry-backed Colorado measure creating a constitutional right to choose natural gas failed about 55-45, intended as the first of many such measures.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Undercuts a gas-industry tool against building electrification and gas bans; watch for copycats elsewhere.
insights.quote: it failed about 55 to 45

insights.claim: An Ann Arbor measure to municipalize the main utility failed by about 3%, while the city's separate clean energy utility experiment continues.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Municipalization pushes remain close-run and costly; incumbent IOU franchises are not easily displaced.

insights.claim: An Arizona measure for a state constitutional ban on taxing miles driven was at about 50.7% and could pass, complicating replacement of gas-tax revenue as transport electrifies.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Signals political resistance to road-usage charges for EVs.

insights.claim: Transit tax measures passed broadly, including Seattle Prop 1 (largest transit service expansion in decades) and a Bay Area regional transit measure, as high gas prices boosted demand for alternatives.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Dedicated transit funding streams support transit agency budgets and bus/rail procurement.
insights.quote: Tuesday was a cost of living election and gas prices are so high

insights.claim: Raman, a left-of-center YIMBY, beat incumbent Karen Bass in the LA mayoral race, which Roberts sees as a major signal for housing and transportation.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Pro-housing LA leadership could accelerate permitting and transit-oriented development.

insights.claim: Zoning-reform measures did worse than transit taxes: California Prop 45 to exempt housing and transit from CEQA review was on track to lose, and Massachusetts Question 7 on small-lot building was a coin flip.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Voters fund transit but resist land-use deregulation; housing supply reform will come mostly via legislatures.

insights.claim: Roberts worries structural forces are pushing energy costs up and new Democratic majorities lack an obvious tool to visibly cut bills, risking voter anger turning on them.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Rising rates remain a political flashpoint, raising the odds of interventionist rate actions against utilities.

insights.claim: Alaska faces some of the worst energy cost spikes, with roughly 22 cents per kWh electricity and MMBtu gas prices that doubled or tripled in a year, making it a prime target for distributed energy and wind.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Alaska is an emerging market for DERs, wind and storage under new leadership.
insights.quote: We have MMBTU prices in Alaska that have doubled, tripled in the last year.

insights.claim: Spears' fastest state levers to cut costs are distributed energy: virtual power plant legislation in every state, community solar, balcony solar, behind-the-meter batteries, removing rooftop solar caps and better net metering.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: DER, VPP and residential storage players could benefit from a wave of 2027 state legislation.
insights.quote: I want to see virtual power plant legislation in every state.

insights.claim: Batteries are undervalued in state capacity rules; states outside PJM such as ERCOT-governed Texas and Alaska can reform battery accreditation directly, while Roberts urges PJM-state governors to team up for PJM reform.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Battery capacity accreditation reform is a direct revenue lever for storage developers.
insights.quote: Batteries are undervalued

insights.claim: Roberts warns of a wave of 'sloppylism', such as rate freezes or gas tax holidays, that look like action but worsen long-term energy and transport finances.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Watch for rate freezes that squeeze utility earnings and capex recovery in newly blue states.
insights.quote: I worry about a wave of sloppylism coming.

insights.claim: With mortgage interest rates around 7.5%, housing supply reforms will take time, so Spears argues states must stack short-term relief with medium- and long-term reforms.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Policy mix likely favors fast DER and grid utilization measures first, with structural reforms later.

insights.claim: EV demand is at a local minimum, suppressed by policy and the California waiver tied up in Trump-administration litigation; Jay Inslee floated state EV leasing programs, and new congressional majorities may revisit EV tariffs.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: EV demand recovery depends on policy catalysts such as tariff changes and state leasing programs.
insights.quote: Right now we're at kind of a local minimum of EV interest

insights.claim: Spears says both a continuing wave and a reversion must be planned for, while Roberts expects some reversion to the mean in R+16-type districts.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Treat 2026 gains as partly transient when underwriting long-dated policy durability.

insights.claim: The Pennsylvania Senate map looks even better for Democrats in 2028, and the Georgia, Texas and North Carolina Senates plus the Texas House are on the target list.
insights.speaker: Caroline Spears (Climate Cabinet)
insights.so_what: Further state legislative gains in 2028 could lock in clean energy policy in large energy states.
insights.quote: the Pennsylvania Senate map looks even better in two years than it did this year

insights.claim: With many Democratic governors likely to run for president, they will race to pass visible cost-cutting energy, transit and housing wins in 2027 to campaign on.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Expect a high volume of state energy-affordability legislation in 2027.
